title: Carbon dioxide removal and net zero: its role now and in the decades ahead

blocks.html: The question is: “Alongside cutting emissions, what part can removing carbon dioxide from the air play in reaching net zero, now and in the decades ahead?”

sentences: Reaching net zero CO2 or net zero GHG emissions requires deep and rapid reductions in gross emissions [2].
The IPCC also finds that deploying carbon dioxide removal (CDR) to counterbalance hard-to-abate residual emissions is unavoidable (high confidence) [2].
CDR will also be necessary to achieve net negative CO2 emissions [2].
Across the IPCC categories of pathways, cuts in gross CO2 and non-CO2 emissions achieve over 80% of net GHG reductions between 2020 and global net zero CO2 [4].
One review states that CDR methods are not a substitute for emissions reductions [5].

It notes that scenarios suggest an 8:2 ratio of effort between reducing CO2 emissions and scaling CO2 removals by mid-century, and that a precautionary approach may suggest even more focus on reductions [5].

blocks.text: Why removals feature in net zero at all

sentences: From a physical science perspective, limiting human-caused global warming to a specific level requires three things: limiting cumulative CO2 emissions, reaching net zero or net negative CO2 emissions, and strongly reducing other GHG emissions [2].
Reaching net zero GHG emissions primarily requires deep reductions in CO2, methane and other GHG emissions, and implies net negative CO2 emissions [2].
Some hard-to-abate residual GHG emissions remain, for example some emissions from agriculture, aviation, shipping and industrial processes [2].
These would need to be counterbalanced by deployment of CDR methods to achieve net zero CO2 or GHG emissions (high confidence) [2].
As a result, net zero CO2 is reached earlier than net zero GHGs (high confidence) [2].
Global net zero CO2 means that remaining anthropogenic CO2 emissions are balanced by durably stored CO2 from anthropogenic removal [2].
Reaching it is a requirement to stabilise CO2-induced global surface temperature increase (high confidence) [2].
The IPCC glossary defines CDR as anthropogenic activities that remove CO2 from the atmosphere and durably store it in geological, terrestrial or ocean reservoirs, or in products [2].
Net zero GHG emissions, if sustained, are projected to result in a gradual decline in global surface temperatures after an earlier peak (high confidence) [2].
Global modelled pathways that reach net zero CO2 and GHG emissions include CDR alongside other measures [2].
These are a transition from fossil fuels without CCS to very low- or zero-carbon energy sources, demand-side measures, improved efficiency, and reduced non-CO2 GHG emissions [2].
For bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), the glossary notes that CO2 can be removed from the atmosphere depending on the total emissions of the supply chain [2].
Current CDR approximates 2 GtCO2 per year, or about 3% of current global net greenhouse gas emissions [5].
Conventional CDR on land is currently estimated to contribute around 2 Gt CO2 of removals per year [4].
Novel CDR, which includes BECCS, direct air carbon capture and storage and enhanced weathering, is currently estimated to contribute around 2 Mt CO2 per year [4].
In 1.5 °C pathways with limited overshoot, mitigation between 2020 and 2030 breaks down as follows: about 70% comes from reducing gross CO2 emissions and about 20% from cutting non-CO2 emissions [4].
About 10% comes from halting deforestation and expanding conventional CDR on land, which nearly doubles the volume of CDR this decade [4].
One analysis describes removals via afforestation and reforestation as playing a critical near-term role in mitigation [4].
Another study states that rapid emissions reductions, including reductions in deforestation-based land emissions, are the dominant source of global mitigation potential in the coming decades [3].
It adds that CDR will also have an important role to play [3].
One review describes three roles for CDR over time [5].
CDR methods can reduce emissions in the near term and compensate for hard-to-abate residual emissions in the medium term [5].
In the long term, they would potentially allow global temperature exceedance to be reversed, but would not compensate for the impacts of overshoot [5].

blocks.text: The role of removals by mid-century and beyond

sentences: Global modelled pathways that limit warming to 1.5 °C (>50%) with no or limited overshoot reach net zero CO2 emissions around 2050, with total GHGs reaching net zero later [2].
Across most 1.5 °C limited-overshoot scenarios, novel CDR methods scale up by mid-century to support net zero CO2, reaching around 4 Gt CO2 (range 2–6) by 2050 [4].
Between 2020 and global net zero CO2 in these pathways, gross CO2 reductions account for 71% of net GHG reductions, while CDR contributes a much smaller 15% [4].
Novel CDR technologies such as direct air carbon capture and storage scale to multi-gigatonne levels by 2050 and beyond, both to balance residual emissions and to draw down warming [4].
Even low estimates of CDR requirements by mid-century imply several gigatons of removals [5].
Across the assessed scenarios, gross greenhouse gas emissions at the year of global net zero CO2 are estimated at 18 (16–21) Gt CO2eq per year [4].
Removals play a larger role after 2050 in the OECD and EU region [4].
There they account for a median of around 43%, 48% and 35% of net GHG reductions across the C1, C2 and C3 pathways respectively [4].

blocks.text: Delay increases reliance on unproven methods

sentences: Delaying net zero CO2 increases the total CDR deployed up to that point [4].
It is 166 Gt CO2 for scenarios reaching net zero by mid-century, 251 Gt CO2 for net zero between 2050 and 2075, and 445 Gt CO2 for net zero later than 2075 [4].
Novel removals are still at a nascent stage of development [4].
They are expected to require both time and investment to ramp up and become a cost-effective part of a mitigation portfolio [4].
The amount of conventional CDR on land is largely consistent across different timings of delayed emissions reductions [4].
By contrast, novel CDR use rises strongly in scenarios with longer net emission halving times [4].
The authors say this shows these scenarios depend on future, unproven CDR technologies when net emissions reductions are delayed [4].

Less stringent climate objectives do not fundamentally change the scale of gross CO2 reductions needed, but merely shift them over time, which the authors say raises questions of intergenerational fairness [4].
Projected CO2 emissions from existing fossil fuel infrastructure without additional abatement would exceed the remaining carbon budget for 1.5 °C (50%) (high confidence) [2].
One analysis identifies a 'CDR gap': CDR efforts proposed by countries fall short of those in integrated assessment model scenarios that limit warming to 1.5 °C [3].
The most ambitious national CDR proposals are close to levels in a low-energy demand scenario that combines the most-limited CDR scaling with aggressive near-term emissions reductions [3].
Many countries propose to expand land-based removals [3].
However, none yet commit to substantively scaling novel methods such as BECCS, biochar or direct air carbon capture and storage [3].
When net zero is reached for a given sector or region depends on several factors (high confidence) [2].
These are the potential to reduce emissions and to undertake CDR, the associated costs, and the availability of policy mechanisms to balance emissions and removals [2].
Scaling CDR will require advances in policymaking and governance, including strict monitoring to ensure removals are durable, additional and do not compete with emission reduction efforts [5].
Many have discussed separate policy tracks for reductions and removals [5].
The aim is to avoid the risk that longer-term ambitions for CDR dilute short-term efforts to reduce emissions [5].
Emerging compliance markets will need to deal with permanence and with how to govern liabilities for removals that expire after a certain period, such as afforestation and reforestation [5].
For BECCS, sustainability concerns include competition for land, impacts on food prices and impacts on biodiversity [4].
Without policy support, one review judges it seems unlikely that niche voluntary markets can sustain novel CDR in the long term [5].
The firmest finding is that deep cuts in gross emissions do most of the work toward net zero [2, 4].
Even so, CDR to counterbalance hard-to-abate residual emissions is unavoidable (high confidence) [2, 4].
Today, removals are almost entirely conventional land-based methods of around 2 Gt CO2 per year, while novel methods contribute around 2 Mt CO2 per year [4].
In the 1.5 °C pathways, the near-term contribution of removals comes mainly from land, at about 10% of net reductions this decade [4].
Novel CDR then scales to gigatonne levels by mid-century, and more is needed the longer emissions reductions are delayed [4].
Countries' current CDR proposals fall short of 1.5 °C scenario levels, and none yet commit to substantively scaling novel methods [3].
The sources treat removal as a complement to emission cuts, not a substitute [4, 5].
It depends on nascent technologies, sustainability safeguards and governance that ensures removals are durable and additional [4, 5].
